title: Building with CMake
objectives: Build a project of several files with CMake.

screens.title: A project of several files
screens.prose: CMake and the compiler run on a desk machine, not in this app; here we read their sessions. In lesson 1 you built one file with `g++`. A pricing project splits into a library, a program and tests.
screens.question: Tap every file the compiler turns into an object file.

hints.text: Which files hold code that runs, and which only declare it?
A header is pasted into each `.cpp` that writes `#include` for it.
The three `.cpp` files: `pricer.cpp`, `main.cpp` and `test_pricer.cpp`.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The compiler takes `.cpp` files, one at a time.

byKey.hdr: You added `pricer.h`. A header is never compiled alone: each `.cpp` that includes it compiles its declarations.
byKey.p-i-h: A header is never compiled alone: each `.cpp` that includes it compiles its declarations.
byKey.p-c: CMake reads `CMakeLists.txt`; the compiler never sees it.

explain.text: Each `.cpp` is compiled on its own into an object file, and the linker joins them. Typing the `g++` line for three files, the include folder and the flags by hand soon goes wrong. **CMake** reads `CMakeLists.txt` and writes those commands for you.

screens.prose: Here is the project's `CMakeLists.txt`. Each command builds or wires up a **target**: a library or a program. Read it line by line, guessing from the names.
screens.question: Tap the two lines that each create a target.

hints.text: Look for the commands whose names start with `add_`.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. A target is created by a command that starts with `add_`.

byKey.link: Line 11 connects two targets that exist already. It creates nothing new.
byKey.l11: Line 11 connects two targets that exist already. It creates nothing new.
byKey.l8: Line 8 tells the `pricing` target where its headers are; it creates nothing.
byKey.l2: `project` names the whole project, not a target to build.
byKey.l4: Line 4 sets the C++ standard for every target.

explain.text: Line 7 makes a library `pricing` from `pricer.cpp`, and line 10 a program `main`. Line 8 says users of `pricing` find headers in `include/`, and line 11 links `main` against it. Lines 1 to 5 fix the CMake version, the project name and C++17.

screens.title: Configure, then build
screens.prose: Two commands build the project. `cmake -S . -B build` **configures**: it reads `CMakeLists.txt` and writes build files into `build/`. `cmake --build build` runs the compiler and linker. Sources stay clean; every generated file lands in `build/`, an **out-of-source build**.

screens.question: Tap the line where the pricing code joins `main.cpp`.

hints.text: Joining compiled pieces is the linker's job.
Two lines say Linking. Which one makes `main`?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the line that links the program `main`.

byKey.lib: Line 8 packs `pricer.o` into the library file. `main.cpp` is not involved yet.
byKey.l7: Line 7 compiles `pricer.cpp` alone. Nothing is joined there.
byKey.l10: Line 10 compiles `main.cpp` alone; its calls into the library are still unresolved.
byKey.l1: That is the configure step. No code is compiled or joined.

explain.text: The library is compiled and packed first, then `main.cpp` is compiled, and line 11 links the two. CMake chose that order from `target_link_libraries`. The program lives in `build/`, so you run `./build/main`.

screens.title: Rebuilding after an edit
screens.prose: You change one line of `src/main.cpp` and run `cmake --build build` again. You do not configure again: `build/` remembers the setup, and CMake reconfigures by itself if `CMakeLists.txt` changes.
screens.question: How many `.cpp` files does the second build compile?

hints.text: Which source files changed since the last build?
`pricer.cpp` and its object file are untouched.
Only `main.cpp` is compiled again, then `main` is relinked.

feedback.correct: Only the edited file, then a fresh link.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. CMake compiles only what changed.

byKey.two: `pricer.cpp` did not change, so its object file is reused. Only `main.cpp` is compiled.
byKey.zero: `main.cpp` changed, so it must be compiled again before `main` is relinked.

explain.text: The build tool compares file times: only `main.cpp` is newer than its object file. So it compiles one file and relinks `main`. On a project of 200 files that turns minutes into seconds, which is why projects split into many files.

screens.title: A header and its source
screens.prose: The header `rates.h` declares three functions; this app has placed it above your file, as `#include` would. Write the matching definitions in `rates.cpp`. `namespace pricing` groups the library's names, as `std` does. Continuous rates: the forward is $S e^{rt}$ and each cash flow is discounted by $e^{-rt}$.

lines: double forward_price(double spot, double r, double t);

screens.question: Define `forward_price` and `present_value`.

hints.text: Copy each declaration from the header and give it a body.
The forward is the spot grown at the rate: `spot * std::exp(r * t)`.
`forward_price` returns `spot * std::exp(r * t)`. `present_value` loops over the cash flows, adding `cash[i] * discount_factor(r, times[i])`.

feedback.correct: Declarations in the header, definitions in the source.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the first failing test or the compiler's message.

byKey.compile: If the message says undefined symbol, a declared function has no definition with the same name and parameter types. Copy the declaration from the header exactly.
byKey.test-4: Three flows of 5, 5 and 105 at 4% give about 102.55. Discount each by `std::exp(-r * t)` with its own time.

explain.text: The header promises the functions exist; the `.cpp` keeps the promise. Other files include only the header, so they compile without seeing these bodies. If a definition were missing, the compile would pass and the link would fail, which the next screen shows.

screens.question: Fix `daycount.cpp` so it links and the tests pass.

hints.text: Compare the definition of `year_fraction` with the declaration in the header.
The header has two parameters; the definition has one.
Define `double year_fraction(int days, int basis)` and return `static_cast<double>(days) / basis`.

feedback.correct: Signatures match, so the linker finds the function.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the first failing test or the linker's message.

byKey.compile: Still an undefined symbol: the definition's parameter types must match `year_fraction(int, int)` exactly.
byKey.test-1: 90 days on a 360 basis is 0.25. If you got 0.2466, the basis is still fixed at 365.
byKey.test-2: 73 / 365 is 0.2. If you got 0, you divided two `int`s: convert with `static_cast<double>`.

explain.text: C++ allows two functions with one name and different parameters, so `year_fraction(int)` was a separate function. `accrued` asked for `year_fraction(int, int)`, which nothing defined. The compiler trusted the header; only the linker could see the gap.

screens.title: Debug and Release
screens.prose: `cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release` turns the optimiser on with `-O2`. A Debug build, `-DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug`, keeps every variable for the debugger and optimises nothing. Desks keep one build folder for each.

state.caption: Pricing 1,000 options on a 500-step tree, one laptop

screens.question: How many times faster is the Release build?

hints.text: Divide the Debug time by the Release time.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the slower time by the faster one.

byKey.inv: You divided Release by Debug. The question asks how many times faster, so put the slower time on top.
byKey.diff: You subtracted. A speed-up is a ratio: 1.28 / 0.16.

explain.text: The optimiser keeps values in registers and inlines small functions, which here buys a factor of 8. Time only Release builds, and never compare a Debug C++ time with Python. `cpp-pricing` times the binomial pricer this way against Python.

screens.title: Found the header, lost the code
screens.prose:
A colleague's `CMakeLists.txt` ends like this, and the build fails.

```cmake
add_library(pricing src/pricer.cpp)
target_include_directories(pricing PUBLIC include)
add_executable(main src/main.cpp)
target_include_directories(main PRIVATE include)
```

lines: collect2: error: ld returned 1 exit status
params.title: Terminal

screens.question: What is wrong?

options.text: `main` sees the header but is never linked with `pricing`: add `target_link_libraries(main PRIVATE pricing)`

options.why: `main.cpp` compiled at 75%, so the header was found. The error comes from the linker, after compiling.
That would link, but it compiles `pricer.cpp` a second time inside `main` and makes the library pointless.
A missing standard gives compile errors in `main.cpp`. This failure is in the link.

hints.text: Did `main.cpp` compile?
The error comes from `ld`, the linker: a function was declared but its code was never joined in.
Including a header gives declarations only. `target_link_libraries` joins the library's code.

feedback.correct: Headers declare; linking supplies the code.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which tool printed the error, the compiler or the linker?

byKey.hdr: `main.cpp` compiled, so the header was found. The linker could not find the code behind it.
byKey.src: That compiles `pricer.cpp` twice, once for the library and once for `main`. Link the library instead.

explain.text: The header let `main.cpp` compile, but the code for `binomial_call` sits in `libpricing.a`, and nothing joined it. `target_link_libraries(main PRIVATE pricing)` links it. It also passes on `pricing`'s `PUBLIC` include folder, so line 4 can go.

screens.prose:
The pattern behind every `CMakeLists.txt` you will meet:

```cmake
add_library(name files...)          # a library target
target_include_directories(name PUBLIC include)
add_executable(name files...)       # a program target
target_link_libraries(user PRIVATE used...)
add_library(name INTERFACE)         # header-only
```
`PUBLIC` passes a setting on to every target that links this one; `PRIVATE` keeps it in.
screens.question: A new `greeks` library calls functions from `pricing`, and `main` calls `greeks`. Which lines link it all?

options.why: This often links, but `greeks` itself never says it needs `pricing`. Every other user of `greeks` must then remember it.
That finds headers only. The code of `pricing` still has to be linked.
That says `pricing` needs `greeks`, the wrong way round.

hints.text: Each target should state what it uses itself.

feedback.correct: Each target names what it uses.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Who uses whom?

explain.text: `greeks` uses `pricing`, so it links it, `PUBLIC` because its headers mention pricing types. `main` then links only `greeks` and receives `pricing` through it. A header-only library has no `.cpp`, so it is `INTERFACE`: it only passes on its include folder.

screens.prose: A colleague clones the pricing project and wants to run `main` built for timing.
screens.question: Put the steps in order.

hints.text: Configuring writes the build files that the build step uses.
Running needs the program, which only the build step makes.
Folder, configure, build, run; after an edit, build again without configuring.

feedback.correct: Configure once, build after every edit.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each step needs what the one before produced.

explain.text: Configure reads `CMakeLists.txt` and fixes the build type; build compiles and links; then the program exists to run. After an edit only `cmake --build build` is needed, and it recompiles just `pricer.cpp`.

screens.title: One library, many tools
screens.prose:
A desk keeps one pricing library that a risk report, a P&L tool and a backtester all link. A new joiner runs `git status` after their first build.

```text
Untracked files:
  build/
```
screens.question: What should they do with `build/`?

options.text: Add `build/` to `.gitignore`: anyone can rebuild it from the sources and `CMakeLists.txt`
Commit it, so colleagues need not compile
options.why: Its object files suit one compiler and one machine, and change on every build. Commit the recipe, not the output.
Files in `build/` are rewritten on every configure, so the edit would vanish. Change `CMakeLists.txt`.
`CMakeLists.txt` is the source of every build. Without it nobody can configure again.

hints.text: Can the folder be made again from what is in the repository?
`cmake -S . -B build` recreates it from `CMakeLists.txt`.

feedback.correct: Version the recipe; ignore what it produces.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Is anything in `build/` impossible to regenerate?

byKey.commit: Build output depends on the machine and changes on every build. The git course's rule applies: keep generated files out.

explain.text: `build/` is fully generated, so it belongs in `.gitignore`, as the git course did with data and secrets. Every tool links the one `pricing` target, so a fix in the library reaches all three after a rebuild. That library, with tests, is what `cpp-pricing` builds.

ideas: A project splits into `.cpp` files compiled one at a time; headers declare, sources define, and the linker joins the objects.
`cmake -S . -B build` configures and `cmake --build build` compiles what changed; time only Release builds.

formula.name: Build and run
formula.note: Add `-DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release` when you configure a build for timing.

summary.trap: Including a header is not linking: without `target_link_libraries` the build fails with an undefined reference.

quiz.prose: To add `-Wall`, you open `build/CMakeFiles/main.dir/flags.make` and add it there. Later a colleague changes `CMakeLists.txt`.
quiz.question: What happens to your flag?

options.why: Files in `build/` are generated. The next configure rewrites them from `CMakeLists.txt`.
CMake never writes back to your sources.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Where does `build/` come from?

explain.text: Everything in `build/` comes from `CMakeLists.txt`. Put the flag there instead: `target_compile_options(main PRIVATE -Wall)`.

quiz.prose: A one-off script, `vol.cpp`, reads closes and prints their volatility. It has no other files.
quiz.question: Does it need CMake?

options.text: Yes: C++ cannot build without CMake
options.why: CMake only writes compiler commands. For one file you can type the one command yourself.
A single program has nothing to share, so there is no library to make.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. What does CMake add for a single file?

explain.text: CMake earns its keep with several files, libraries, tests and build types. A single file is one `g++` line, as in lesson 1.

quiz.prose: A dashboard shows Python 4.1 s, C++ Debug 1.3 s and C++ Release 0.16 s for the same pricer.
quiz.question: Which claim is fair?

options.text: C++ (Release) is about 26 times faster than Python here
C++ is about 3 times faster than Python here
options.why: That uses the Debug build, which is not optimised. Timings must come from Release builds.

options.text: C++ is between 3 and 26 times faster, depending on luck
options.why: The gap is the build type, not luck. Only the Release build is a fair timing.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which C++ build would ship?

explain.text: 4.1 / 0.16 is about 26. A Debug build switches the optimiser off, so its time says little about real speed.

quiz.prose: `stats.h` is header-only: every function in it is `inline`, and there is no `stats.cpp`.
quiz.question: How do you declare it in CMake?

options.why: A normal library needs source files to compile. A header alone compiles to nothing.
An `INTERFACE` library is a target with no code of its own; linking it passes on its include folder.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. What does a library with no `.cpp` have to pass on?

explain.text: An `INTERFACE` target compiles nothing. Linking it, `target_link_libraries(main PRIVATE stats)`, hands `main` its include folder and settings.
